How Shared Inference Clusters Actually Fail

Most teams assume that a benchmark number on a vendor's slide will translate directly into production throughput. It rarely does, and the gap is almost never about the model itself. It is about everything surrounding the model: batching policy, scheduler fairness, and the assumptions a cluster operator made about how traffic would actually arrive.

When we first stood up a shared inference cluster, our benchmark suite reported numbers that looked excellent in isolation. Every request was synthetic, every prompt length was identical, and every client waited patiently for its turn. None of that resembled the real traffic we saw a week later, when a dozen internal teams began routing production workloads through the same pool of GPUs.

The first failure mode was head-of-line blocking. A handful of long-context requests could stall a queue of short, latency-sensitive calls behind them, because the scheduler had no concept of priority beyond arrival order. The fix was not a bigger cluster. It was a scheduler that understood the shape of the requests it was serving.

The second failure mode was memory fragmentation under bursty load. KV cache allocation that looked fine at steady state fell apart the moment concurrency spiked, because the allocator was never tested against the kind of traffic pattern production actually produces. Synthetic benchmarks rarely reproduce this, because they rarely reproduce burstiness at all.

The lesson generalizes beyond this one cluster. A benchmark number describes a benchmark. It does not describe your traffic, your tenants, or your failure modes. If you want a number that predicts production behavior, you have to build the benchmark out of your own traffic shape, not someone else's idealized one. That is the only way the number means anything at all when the pager goes off at two in the morning and everyone is asking why the dashboard disagrees with the slide from procurement.
